entries.text: The next wave of AI innovation is happening now. Join the developers, researchers, engineers, and industry leaders driving that progress at PyTorch Day China 2026, taking place December 12 in Beijing. Co-hosted by Alibaba Cloud, AMD, and the PyTorch Foundation, this community-driven event brings together the people and technologies shaping the future of open source AI. Whether you’re building AI applications, optimizing models, advancing hardware acceleration, or contributing to open source projects, PyTorch Day China offers valuable opportunities to gain new insights, exchange ideas, and connect with the community. Register now to explore cutting-edge advancements in training, inference, responsible AI, and more. Featured Sessions Get inspired by technical presentations from leading experts and innovators. A few featured sessions include: Accelerating PyTorch on AMD GPUs with FlyDSL – Xiaobing Zhang, Shijie Feng, and Xudong Yuan, AMD Beyond KV Cache: Mooncake Evolves from Inference Caching to Agentic AI Data Infrastructure – Teng Ma, Mooncake Maintainer Finish RL Training Faster: Bitwise-Identical Rollout and Training Across NVIDIA and AMD GPUs – Ao Shen, Inferact PyTorch on RISC-V: Upstream Support and Deployment with RuyiAI – Hongbin Zhang & Yixuan Chen, Institute of Software, Chinese Academy of Sciences View the full schedule. entries.summary: TL;DR At the Singapore vLLM meetup, engineers from Inferact, NVIDIA, and Alibaba Cloud showcased how the community is advancing open source AI inference through pipeline parallelism optimizations, agent-written…
entries.text: TL;DR At the Singapore vLLM meetup, engineers from Inferact, NVIDIA, and Alibaba Cloud showcased how the community is advancing open source AI inference through pipeline parallelism optimizations, agent-written kernels, real-time multimodal world models, and day-zero support for next-generation hardware like NVIDIA’s Vera Rubin platform. Introduction On November 13, 2026, the vLLM community gathered at SGInnovate in Singapore for a half-day technical meetup hosted by Inferact and NVIDIA. Engineers from Inferact, NVIDIA and Alibaba Cloud, together with vLLM-Omni contributors, shared what they are building right now, from high-throughput prefill and RL training to running vLLM on workstation-class Blackwell GPUs and NVIDIA’s Vera Rubin platform. vLLM, born at UC Berkeley and now hosted under the PyTorch Foundation, serves hundreds of model architectures across a wide range of accelerators. Two themes ran through the day: squeezing throughput out of communication-bound layouts, and using AI agents to write and tune kernels. Highlights from the Meetup 1. Optimizing Pipeline Parallelism for High-Throughput Prefill in vLLM Thien Tran, Member of Technical Staff from Inferact made the case for pipeline parallelism (PP) as a throughput layout for prefill. In agentic traffic, one turn carries roughly 100K input tokens (about 95% cached), so a 3 s time-to-first-token (TTFT) target for 5K new tokens leaves a per-token budget about 33× tighter than decode’s. On MiniMax-M3.1-Flash on 2× GB
entries.title: vLLM Singapore Meetup: Faster Prefill, Agent-Written Kernels and the Road to Vera Rubin

entries.summary: TL;DR With Torch-TensorRT 2.15 and ExecuTorch 1.6 you can compile a PyTorch model with TensorRT, save it as an ExecuTorch program, and run it from C++ or Python without loading...
entries.text: TL;DR With Torch-TensorRT 2.15 and ExecuTorch 1.6 you can compile a PyTorch model with TensorRT, save it as an ExecuTorch program, and run it from C++ or Python without loading torch. You stay in PyTorch the whole way, and whatever TensorRT can’t handle can still run on the GPU. On an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano it comes within 4% of the fastest TensorRT setup we measured, in both speed and memory. A 3.6-billion-parameter policy fits on the 8 GB board, where PyTorch eager mode runs out of memory. You compile with one pip install "torch_tensorrt[executorch]". To run, the robot needs only ExecuTorch and a small TensorRT backend, not PyTorch. We talked about this work at PyTorch Conference 2026: Deploying Robot Policies Across Many Targets with ExecuTorch. https://pytorch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/et-trt.mp4 GR00T 1.7 (3B) on a Jetson Orin Nano 8GB: about 200 ms per action chunk. Why is it hard to run a PyTorch model with TensorRT on a robot? A robot runs its models on its own computer, like NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor or a custom board, and they have to finish on time. A policy, the model that decides what the robot does next, returns a short plan at a time, called an action chunk, say 50 actions. If the next chunk isn’t ready when the robot finishes the current one, the robot stops and waits. And everything shares the same memory: the CPU, the GPU, the cameras and every model. entries.summary: The PyTorch Foundation is proud to celebrate the winners and nominees of the fourth annual PyTorch Foundation Contributor Awards!
entries.text: The PyTorch Foundation is proud to celebrate the winners and nominees of the fourth annual PyTorch Foundation Contributor Awards! Presented on the keynote stage at PyTorch Conference 2026 in San Jose, California, these awards recognize the individuals whose dedication, innovation, and contributions help advance open source projects and strengthen the communities around them. 2026 Awards at a Glance 15 Award Winners | 11 Nominees | 9 Award Categories | 3 New Categories This year marks another milestone for the program, with 15 award winners, up from 11 in 2025, recognizing outstanding contributions across PyTorch Foundation-hosted projects, including PyTorch, vLLM, Ray, and DeepSpeed. Expanding Recognition Across the PyTorch Ecosystem As the PyTorch Foundation’s community continues to grow, the Contributor Awards have evolved to reflect the diverse ways individuals contribute to its projects. In 2026, three new award categories were introduced: Knowledge Enhancer: Celebrating contributors who make knowledge more accessible through documentation, tutorials, and educational resources. Bug Buster: Recognizing those who identify, report, and resolve bugs that improve project quality and reliability. Catalyst: Honoring contributions that improve developer workflows, automation, infrastructure, and AI-supported development. entries.summary: PyTorch Foundation Ambassadors bring people together to learn, share technical knowledge and contribute to PyTorch Foundation projects and the wider open-source AI ecosystem.
entries.text: PyTorch Foundation Ambassadors bring people together to learn, share technical knowledge and contribute to PyTorch Foundation projects and the wider open-source AI ecosystem. In this November roundup, we highlight some of our ambassadors’ activities, including local meetups, university sessions, technical articles and practical learning resources. PyTorch Community Meetup in Kampala On September 19, Pacifique Mugisho organized an in-person PyTorch East Africa community meetup at Makerere University in Kampala, Uganda, in collaboration with the IndabaX Makerere Student Chapter and the IEEE Computer Society Makerere Student Branch. The event received 103 registrations and welcomed 32 attendees. Talks explored retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), external knowledge integration and advanced retrieval techniques. Pacifique also led a practical workshop covering embeddings, semantic search and how these components can be combined in PyTorch-based applications. An interactive quiz gave participants another way to engage with the material. Following the event, the community gained 20 WhatsApp members and four LinkedIn members. The gathering also laid the groundwork for further in-person meetups. Technical talks and hands-on learning at the PyTorch East Africa community meetup at Makerere University, Kampala. entries.summary: TL;DR Helion now uses compile-time heuristics that analyze a kernel’s IR and dataflow to pick fast settings without slow autotuning.
entries.text: TL;DR Helion now uses compile-time heuristics that analyze a kernel’s IR and dataflow to pick fast settings without slow autotuning. It classifies the kernel as matmul, reduction, or pointwise and chooses block sizes, warps, and stages, giving near-autotuned speed for free. Introduction Helion, PyTorch’s domain-specific language (DSL) for performance portable machine learning kernels, relies heavily on autotuning for its performance. Autotuning time can be a major bottleneck: for example, a previous team tuning a single paged-attention kernel across 72 shapes spent 10 hours in Helion’s quick mode, and 25 at full effort. To address these issues, we’ve developed a set of heuristics that read a kernel’s IR and dataflow at compile time and emit a config directly, without any autotuning. We classify kernels into broad families based on the operations they contain – matmul, reduction, or pointwise – and apply a family-specific heuristic to each. These families are intentionally general: the matmul heuristic, for example, looks for any kernel containing a matmul operation such as hl.dot or torch.baddbmm, not just standard m-n-k matrix multiplications. These are designed to be generic and apply broadly to custom kernels that users may write. Highlights: Autotuner Heuristics. Our heuristics cover a large set of kernels, including GEMM, reductions, and even linear attention. Linear attention. Over 96 kernel-and-shape cells spanning nine linear-attention variants, the computed config be
entries.title: Fast by Default: Compile-Time Heuristics for Helion Kernels

entries.summary: TL;DR With help from AI coding agents, our two-person team integrated SGLang with IBM Spyre in less than a week, building a plugin of roughly 1,500 lines.
entries.text: TL;DR With help from AI coding agents, our two-person team integrated SGLang with IBM Spyre in less than a week, building a plugin of roughly 1,500 lines. Existing Spyre support in PyTorch and SGLang’s clear extension points made it straightforward to reuse the hardware code. SGLang delivered about 3.6× the throughput of the reference PyTorch inference implementation using torch-spyre. It was also on par with vLLM on the workloads measured for Granite 3.3 8B and Gemma 4 26B A4B. Prefix sharing through RadixCache worked without any Spyre-specific changes. We work on IBM’s Spyre accelerator and wanted to make SGLang‘s serving stack, including its built-in prefix sharing, available to Spyre users. In less than a week, the two of us used AI-assisted development to integrate SGLang into IBM Spyre with a plugin of just ~1,500 lines of code. A key factor was building on existing PyTorch hardware support and SGLang’s well-defined extension points. This allowed the two of us, alongside our AI coding agents, to integrate a new accelerator into SGLang in a remarkably short time. The AI coding agents used existing PyTorch implementations of Spyre operations as reference code and adapted the integration code to SGLang’s backend interfaces. Their work focused on connecting the existing hardware support to the new serving framework. Spyre and the starting point Spyre is IBM’s accelerator for enterprise AI inference. It integrates using torch-spyre, which registers Spyre as a PyTorch device
entries.title: Integrating SGLang into Spyre in Under a Week with AI

entries.summary: TL;DR Scaling pretraining for a ~1-trillion-parameter Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model on shared, public infrastructure was previously considered unfeasible due to unique architectural and interconnect bottlenecks.
entries.text: TL;DR Scaling pretraining for a ~1-trillion-parameter Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model on shared, public infrastructure was previously considered unfeasible due to unique architectural and interconnect bottlenecks. However, by leveraging the fine-grained flexibility of PyTorch and TorchTitan, the EUROPA consortium successfully unlocked frontier-scale training on JUPITER, boosting throughput from 90 to ~1,300 tokens/sec per GPU across 384 NVIDIA GH200 GPUs per DP replica (96 nodes) as part of the EuroHPC Frontier AI Grand Challenge. The EuroHPC Frontier AI Grand Challenge was designed to prove that sovereign, open-source AI could compete at frontier levels using shared public resources. As part of that process, we – as the EUROPA consortium, formed by Domyn and Fraunhofer IAIS and IIS – were selected to an open European Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model of at least 400B parameters, support for all 24 official EU languages, and strict compliance with the EU AI Act. In this post, we describe how we scaled pretraining to 1T MoE on JUPITER, the EuroHPC exascale supercomputer hosted at Forschungszentrum Jülich, proving that public infrastructure can indeed sustain frontier scale. entries.summary: TL;DR PyTorch models now run in the web browser on the GPU through ExecuTorch, with no conversion to another framework’s format.
entries.text: TL;DR PyTorch models now run in the web browser on the GPU through ExecuTorch, with no conversion to another framework’s format. You export with torch.export to an ExecuTorch .pte file, and the same file runs in any WebGPU browser via ExecuTorch’s new WebGPU backend. It works across a broad range of models: LLMs (e.g. Llama 3.2, Qwen3, Gemma 3), vision-language (e.g. SmolVLM), segmentation, depth, object detection, super-resolution and speech-to-text (e.g. Whisper). Everything runs locally in the tab, and no data leaves the device. Try it in the ExecuTorch WebGPU Playground. On the same machine, WebGPU is 4–7× faster than ExecuTorch’s CPU path (Webassembly + XNNPACK) on prefill and 2–10× faster on decode. Why the Browser? The web is the largest deployment surface with billions of users on Chrome, Firefox and Safari. Browser inference ensures privacy by keeping users’ prompts, model inputs, and outputs on the user’s device rather than the server. This reduces network latency, enables offline use-cases, and lowers server-side inference costs. With the ExecuTorch WebGPU backend, PyTorch models get a native path to GPU-accelerated inference in WebGPU-enabled browsers on desktop, laptop and mobile. WebGPU, the modern successor to WebGL, provides native compute shaders, shared memory, storage buffers, and barriers, making it viable for high-performance ML inference directly in the browser. entries.summary: TL;DR We serve Meta’s Muse Spark Open, an 816B-parameter mixture-of-experts model, on a single TPU v7 host of four chips, with SGLang running on the TorchTPU PyTorch backend.
entries.text: TL;DR We serve Meta’s Muse Spark Open, an 816B-parameter mixture-of-experts model, on a single TPU v7 host of four chips, with SGLang running on the TorchTPU PyTorch backend. At the center is a megakernel: all 62 layers of a decode or verify step run as one Pallas program, and every weight load, KV read and cross-device transfer is pipelined behind compute. The rest of the work falls into three groups: faster decode steps (collective folding, a max-free attention loop that pipelines its KV chunks, an expert loop that keeps register spills off its common path, and DFlash2 speculative decoding), more KV cache per chip (sequence-on-lane KV layout in the megakernel, and L2 HiCache on TPU with session-aware eviction), and faster prefill (a fused MoE kernel and sequence parallelism). Decode speed. The megakernel halves the time per output token for one or two concurrent requests, where it helps the most; the gain narrows as concurrency grows. Its verify step runs within 1.5–1.7× of the time it takes just to stream its weights from HBM. AgentX. On the 1M-context version of SemiAnalysis’s agentic-coding benchmark, our curve runs from 433 output tokens/s per request at 6,101 tokens/s per chip to 25,906 tokens/s per chip at 95 tokens/s per request (Figure 1).
